title: Rigorous Yet Sustainable Human Reviews in the AI Era
gist: Drawing on Nobel economist Joel Mokyr's 'knowledge feedback loop' theory, speaker Artie Shevchenko argues AI-generated code creates 'deceptive correctness' and a review-volume crisis that erodes team understanding ('cognitive debt'); his proposed fix — letting code owners rely on AI-only review for their own PRs — only works if most engineers are owners and teams stay small.

insights.claim: Citing 2025 Nobel-winning economic historian Joel Mokyr, Shevchenko argues technological progress only becomes permanent when practice and deep theoretical understanding continuously feed into each other, forming a 'knowledge feedback loop' — and today AI has the potential to both strengthen and break that loop.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: A durable macro-framework for evaluating any AI-adoption program: ask whether it is reinforcing genuine understanding or just accelerating output while eroding the theory-practice loop that makes progress permanent.
insights.quote: Today, AI has the potential to strengthen the knowledge feedback loop, but it also has the potential to break it.

insights.claim: AI doesn't actually understand anything — it generates tokens, creating an illusion of understanding; without a human in the loop, teams risk accumulating knowledge without real understanding, breaking the feedback loop.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: A sharp, high-conviction warning against treating AI-generated explanations or code as validated understanding — directly relevant to any organization scaling AI-assisted development without proportional human review capacity.
insights.quote: AI doesn’t really understand anything; it generates tokens, creating an illusion of understanding

themes.theme: Cognitive debt: AI's hidden organizational cost

insights.claim: 'Cognitive debt' is defined as the erosion of a team's shared understanding of the system it works on, and AI amplifies this problem specifically by increasing the volume of code changes requiring review.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Introduces a named, trackable organizational-risk metric analogous to technical debt but for team knowledge — a concept investors evaluating AI-adoption maturity in engineering orgs should probe for.

insights.claim: Rigorous code review is not just a skill or habit but a muscle with hard physiological limits — it can be trained, but there is a ceiling to how much review volume any reviewer can sustainably handle.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Implies that AI-driven code-volume growth cannot be solved purely by 'training reviewers harder' — structural changes to review policy (not just individual skill-building) are required.
insights.quote: Rigorous code reviews are not just a skill or a habit; they’re also a muscle

themes.theme: Review policy design under AI-driven volume

insights.claim: For non-trivial changes, Shevchenko lays out three options — rigorous review (harder than ever with AI), skimming (which accumulates cognitive debt fast), or a 'coding first, AI second' approach where a spike plus specification is given to AI for proposed fixes, which the developer then selectively reviews having already built deep understanding from writing the spike.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: The 'coding first, AI second' pattern is a concrete, actionable review workflow for engineering leaders trying to preserve reviewer understanding while still leveraging AI suggestions.

insights.claim: The most impactful optimization Shevchenko proposes is letting code owners rely on AI-only review for their own pull requests — notifying other owners instead of requiring peer review, with AI effectively rubberstamping the merge — while non-owner PRs still get peer review.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: A concrete, high-leverage policy lever (AI-only review for code owners) that engineering-productivity vendors and internal platform teams could adopt directly to cut review bottlenecks.
insights.quote: Instead of peer review, you notify other owners, AI rubberstamps it, and you merge it.

insights.claim: The owner-AI-review policy only meaningfully improves velocity if most engineers on a team are code owners and the team is small; if only a few engineers hold ownership, those few still spend nearly all their time reviewing AI-generated changes from non-owners, so the policy's benefit collapses.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: A critical caveat that prevents naive over-application of the policy — investors or leaders evaluating 'AI-approved code' claims from vendors/teams should check team size and ownership-distribution before trusting reported velocity gains.

insights.claim: Expanding code ownership broadly to make the AI-review policy work is constrained by the risk of compromising architectural integrity — ownership cannot simply be handed out to everyone without a trade-off.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Flags an explicit tension between review-scalability and architectural governance that any org adopting broad code-ownership models must actively manage.

themes.theme: Specific risks of reviewing AI-generated code

insights.claim: The sheer volume of incoming AI-generated code changes is, in Shevchenko's own ranking, the dominant reviewer challenge — far outweighing other issues — because every reviewer has a personal fatigue threshold beyond which the mental cost of processing additional reviews grows exponentially.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Establishes review-volume (not code quality per se) as the primary bottleneck metric to track when assessing whether an AI-coding rollout is sustainable for an engineering org.

insights.claim: AI-generated code exhibits 'deceptive correctness' — it looks more plausible at first glance than human-written code, meaning spotting subtle flaws under that polished surface actually requires more mental effort than reviewing traditional code, not less.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Directly counters the common assumption that AI-written code is easier or faster to review because it 'looks clean' — a key risk factor for teams scaling AI code generation without adjusting review rigor.

insights.claim: AI defaults to adding new code rather than simplifying or removing what already exists, so spotting opportunities to streamline or refactor still requires a reviewer's deep understanding of the broader codebase — a capability AI does not substitute for.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Implies AI-assisted development has a structural bias toward code bloat/accumulation over time unless human reviewers actively counteract it — a long-run maintainability risk for AI-heavy codebases.
